Done. PR **#126** is ready: https://github.com/jreinach-alt/hakuX/pull/126

## The forensics came back negative, and I said so rather than building on it

The brief's hypothesis — that the hold path removes the lane file and only restores it in the process that observed the hold — **is false, and reading the code is enough**. `held_logged=1` is assigned unconditionally on the same line-run as its `rm`, so the hold path self-heals within one process. Two more hypotheses died too: EXIT-trap leakage into `$(...)` (bash doesn't do it — measured on this host), and a third remover elsewhere in the tree (a repo-wide grep yields exactly three sites, all in `dispatcher.sh`).

**I could not name what fired at 16:44.** The lane sandbox refuses to read outside its worktree, so the live `$D/lanes`, `$D/hold` and the dispatcher log were unreachable. That question is still open and `docs/lanes/armpin/NOTES.md` records the two commands that would settle it from a session that can reach the host.

## What I fixed instead

The removal is a whodunnit; the defect is that it was **permanent**. The lane pid file was written twice in a worker's whole life, so any removal took that device out of `serving()` until a restart — that is what turned a transient `rm` into five hours of unpinned pairs.

- `lane_claim` re-asserts every loop tick (after the hold check) — a removal costs one tick, not one restart.
- `lane_release` removes the file only if it still holds **my** pid, so a stale predecessor's EXIT trap cannot evict its live successor. That's the one mechanism fitting every observation, but I've labelled it a hypothesis, not a finding.
- `lane_blind_check` logs `AFFINITY BLIND` once per outage and once on recovery; `_note_blind()` writes the same fact into `$D/splits/`; `status.sh` gives that directory its first reader.

Failing open is unchanged and `ab_compare.py`'s cross-device refusal is untouched.

## Falsification

```
before merge   new: 66 passed, 0 failed   |   old: 49 passed, 17 failed
after merge    new: 85 passed, 0 failed
```

All 17 failures are mine; nothing pre-existing broke. The 3 passing both ways are the labelled controls. Worth flagging: **four of my checks passed both ways on the first run and were vacuous, not controls** — `disp 'lane_claim; ...; [ ! -e f ]'` was satisfied by a file with no `lane_claim` in it, since the missing function failed and "file is absent" then came out true. Chained with `&&`, they fail. That rewrite is why the count is 17 and not 12.

One residual I did not close: re-assertion is per loop tick, and the loop is blocked inside `serve_one` for a whole device run, so a file removed 30s into a 26-minute arm stays missing until it finishes. That needs a background refresher, which is larger than this brief — and the window is now loud rather than silent.
